status_reasoning: Reviewers acknowledge that LOH events were commonly observed and associated with drug resistance, but express concern about the lack of statistical modeling to assess significance. They specifically note: 'The recurring appearance of LOH events that coincide with changes in MIC suggests that they have been positively selected…' but question 'This is a "coincidence", as the authors say, but is it significant?' The reviewers indicate that 'without proper statistics it is not possible to evaluate' whether these patterns represent real selective events or chance occurrences.

Reviewers note the identification of 240 recurrently mutated genes but express major concern about statistical rigor. They state: 'There is very little statistical modeling to assess how likely these combinations of certain mutational patterns are due to real selective events due to specific phenotypic consequences or just by chance' and 'it is hard to know which signals are truly significant.' While the authors report statistical significance (p < 10⁻⁴), reviewers indicate this is insufficient to establish that the recurrent mutations represent true adaptive changes rather than chance events.

Reviewers acknowledge the deletion mutant validation experiments but express dissatisfaction with their scope and conclusiveness. They note: 'This is an experiment that was necessary but surprisingly it was not given the proper weight (it was only a small fraction of the total text), plus it was not as conclusive as one would like regarding the MIC phenotype.' Only 1 of 23 tested genes showed MIC effects, which reviewers imply is insufficient validation of the broader claims about recurrently mutated genes.

Reviewers raise serious concerns about SNP calling accuracy, noting 'The SNP calling accuracy was found to be 87.3% on average' with 'important inter-sample variability, with very poor results observed in half of the tested series (<65% calling accuracy). This is worrying.' They question whether this could be 'due to intra-patient diversity, with different Candida subpopulations being sampled' and state 'these inconsistencies should be listed as an important limitation of the study.' This technical concern undermines confidence in the mutation calls that form the basis of the study.

Reviewers fundamentally challenge the interpretation that observed variants arose during treatment, stating: 'the data suggest that the variants that distinguish C. albicans genomes at different time points did not arise during the sampling window but were largely, maybe entirely, pre-existing (standing variation).' They cite three lines of evidence: '(i) the very considerable genetic diversity (thousands of SNP differences) between isolates of the same strain within the same host, sampled less than a few months apart, in one case on the same day; (ii) the implausible mutation rate that would be needed to explain this variation as newly arising by mutation; and, (iii) the lack of analysis demonstrating that the data shows any signal of "measurable evolution".'

Reviewers do not challenge the findings about aneuploidies being prevalent but transient and not consistently correlated with drug resistance. These observations are presented as descriptive findings and are not among the major concerns raised by reviewers, suggesting implicit acceptance of these claims as adequately supported by the data.

Reviewers acknowledge 'a degree of phenotypic assessment paired with the sequence data' and do not raise specific concerns about the phenotypic variation findings (adhesion, filamentation, virulence). The statement that 'The experimental and sequence analysis methodologies seem to be state of the art' suggests acceptance of these experimental measurements, though the overall interpretation is questioned due to statistical and evolutionary concerns.
